Indian heritage

What is intangible cultural heritage? Meaning and Indian examples

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

Intangible cultural heritage is the living part of culture: practices, performances, knowledge, skills and festivals that communities pass from one generation to the next. It lives in people rather than in buildings or objects. India's examples on the UNESCO list include Vedic chanting, Ramlila, Kutiyattam, Yoga, the Kumbh Mela, Durga Puja in Kolkata and the Garba of Gujarat.

Talaash Heritage runs an oral history and neighbourhood memory lab that teaches students to document a living tradition, online or in person.

Intangible cultural heritage meaning in simple words

Some heritage can be photographed and fenced: a stupa, a fort, a bronze image. Intangible heritage cannot. It is a song a grandmother teaches, the footwork of a dance, the way a potter judges when clay is ready, the order of events at a village festival. It exists only while people keep doing it.

UNESCO's Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, adopted in 2003, defines it as the practices, representations, expressions, knowledge and skills, with their associated instruments, objects and spaces, that communities recognise as part of their cultural heritage. Two ideas sit inside that definition. The community decides what counts, and the heritage is constantly recreated, so it changes as it is passed on. India ratified the Convention in 2005.

Intangible heritage is one half of the wider idea explained in our guide to what cultural heritage is. The other half, the tangible, depends on it more than people think.

The five domains of intangible heritage

The 2003 Convention sorts intangible heritage into five broad domains. Most real traditions cross several of them at once.

  • Oral traditions and expressions, including language as a vehicle of heritage: epics, folk tales, proverbs, chants.
  • Performing arts: music, dance, theatre and puppetry.
  • Social practices, rituals and festive events: fairs, pilgrimages, seasonal festivals, rites of passage.
  • Knowledge and practices concerning nature and the universe: traditional medicine, farming knowledge, water management, astronomy.
  • Traditional craftsmanship: weaving, metalwork, pottery, carving and the skills behind them.

India's elements on the UNESCO intangible heritage list

UNESCO keeps a Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. India has more than a dozen entries on it. The table gives a selection, with the region each comes from. In India the Sangeet Natak Akademi acts as the nodal body for nominations, under the Ministry of Culture.

Durga Puja in KolkataWest BengalFestive event
Garba of GujaratGujaratPerforming arts and festive event

Examples of intangible cultural heritage beyond the UNESCO list

The UNESCO list is a small window. Most of India's intangible heritage will never be nominated, and it matters just as much. Think of the oral epics sung by bards in Rajasthan, the boat songs of Bengal, the harvest dances of the northeast, the knowledge farmers hold about local rice varieties, or the recipes cooked for a single festival in a single town. Our guides to folk dances of India state-wise and traditional crafts of India list many more.

Language is often the deepest layer. When a language loses its last fluent speakers, the songs, place names, jokes and plant names carried in it go too. That is why linguists treat documentation of endangered languages as heritage work, a theme in our session on India's linguistic heritage.

Tangible and intangible heritage: why they cannot be separated

A temple is stone, but the music played at its festivals, the craft guilds that repair its chariot and the calendar that decides when the deity is taken out are intangible. A handloom is wood and thread, but the weaver's skill is what makes it heritage. Take the living practice away and the object becomes a museum piece.

Archaeologists see this too. Pottery shapes and firing techniques at some Indian villages echo forms found in excavated layers centuries old, which is one reason a pottery workshop is a good way to understand both the object and the skill behind it.

How intangible heritage is safeguarded

Safeguarding is not freezing. The aim is to keep a tradition alive and in the hands of its community, not to fix it in one form. Typical measures include documentation (recordings, inventories, written descriptions), support for teachers and apprentices, festivals and platforms for performance, and protection of the spaces a practice needs, such as a forest grove or a market square.

Recording is the part anyone can start with. Interviewing elders, filming a craft step by step and noting local terms creates a record that communities can use. Our oral history and neighbourhood memory lab teaches groups to do this carefully and with consent.

Intangible cultural heritage notes for students

Points to remember for school projects and exams:

  • Definition: living practices, expressions, knowledge and skills that communities recognise as their heritage.
  • International text: UNESCO Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2003. India ratified it in 2005.
  • Five domains: oral traditions, performing arts, social practices and festivals, knowledge about nature, traditional craftsmanship.
  • Indian examples on the UNESCO list: Kutiyattam, Vedic chanting, Ramlila, Yoga, Kumbh Mela, Durga Puja in Kolkata, Garba of Gujarat.
  • Indian nodal agency: Sangeet Natak Akademi, under the Ministry of Culture.

Questions people ask

What is intangible cultural heritage in one line?

Intangible cultural heritage is the living culture that communities pass on by practice and teaching, such as songs, dances, festivals, rituals, crafts skills and traditional knowledge, rather than by buildings or objects.

What are five examples of intangible cultural heritage in India?

Vedic chanting, Kutiyattam Sanskrit theatre from Kerala, Ramlila, the Kumbh Mela and the Garba of Gujarat. All five are on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, along with Yoga and Durga Puja in Kolkata.

When did Garba get UNESCO intangible heritage status?

Garba of Gujarat was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List in December 2023. It followed Durga Puja in Kolkata, inscribed in 2021, and the Kumbh Mela, inscribed in 2017.

Which body handles intangible heritage in India?

The Sangeet Natak Akademi, an autonomous body under the Ministry of Culture, is the nodal agency for intangible cultural heritage. It prepares India's nominations to UNESCO and supports performing arts, while other bodies support crafts, languages and traditional knowledge.

Is yoga intangible cultural heritage?

Yes. Yoga was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2016, recognised as a body of knowledge and practice passed on through teachers and students over many centuries.
